single-d.title: The Initiator
single-d.headline: Take an idea to its next step.
single-d.introduction: When a discussion has not reached a conclusion, you may propose a direction first: what needs to be done, who will take responsibility, and what can start now. In this attempt, moving-forward options received your highest count.
portrait: When something has yet to get started, you may look for the part that can move: set a goal, propose a plan, and give the discussion a next step. This result offers a question for reflection: how do you usually open a way forward when things remain undecided?

Moving things forward focuses on what comes next. When planning a gathering, for example, you might propose two dates and a budget rather than continue a general discussion. Asking for concrete responses can reveal constraints, even before the proposal is final.

This approach can reduce waiting and guesswork. Once the goal is clear, confirming responsibilities and initiating a trial can help work continue. Notice whether you also enjoy turning scattered opinions into an action people are willing to join.

People do not necessarily move at the same pace. Some are still organising their thoughts; others have noticed a risk. Treating silence as agreement too quickly can lead to disagreement and rework later. Ask whether someone objects to the goal or is adding conditions for achieving it.

You can keep your initiative while leaving room to revise a decision: explain what is settled and what remains adjustable, invite affected people to confirm conditions, and agree on a review time. Also recall an occasion when you waited, listened or checked carefully. Your highest count need not become a fixed script for every action.

strengths.title: Make a vague goal concrete
strengths.body: Replace “finish it soon” with what this round should deliver and to what standard. Clear completion criteria make the next step easier to judge.

strengths.title: Find a starting point
strengths.body: When discussion stalls, propose a small, low-cost, adjustable trial. A draft reviewed by the relevant people can inform whether to continue.

strengths.title: Give responsibility a clear owner
strengths.body: Ask who will follow up and when you will review progress. Confirming the assignment with that person helps prevent gaps at handover.

strengths.title: Give opinions something concrete to address
strengths.body: State your suggestion, its reasons and what is open for discussion. Others can add information without guessing your expectations.

strengths.title: Help discussion stay focused
strengths.body: When conversation drifts, ask which issue most needs resolving now. Address the priority and record what will wait.

edges.title: Mistaking silence for agreement
edges.body: Did objections surface only after a quick meeting? Before deciding, ask each affected person to confirm constraints, especially those who have not spoken.

edges.title: Responding before hearing the concern
edges.body: When someone says it may not work, ask which step worries them and what information is needed. Turn the risk into a condition to check before persuading.

edges.title: Starting anew before finishing
edges.body: Before taking up an appealing new plan, check whether the previous task was delivered, handed over or explicitly paused. Starting less can help existing work finish.

edges.title: Pushing others to match your pace
edges.body: When someone needs time to organise information, agree on a response time and provide context. Repeated prompts before information is ready may produce rushed answers and rework.

work: When goals and authority are clear, use initiative to coordinate the next step: record the decision, confirm the owner, and agree on delivery and review times. If work stalls, distinguish missing information, missing resources and unresolved agreement before choosing how to proceed.

Before starting, ask both what counts as complete and what would require a pause. Decisions affecting others’ rights, requiring professional judgement or being difficult to reverse need conditions and authority checked first. Speed still needs a sound basis.
relationships: You may express care through action: finding information, arranging a time or addressing an immediate problem. When the other person wants a solution, initiative can feel supportive. Asking whether they want help with that part makes it more responsive to their needs.

Someone close to you may simply want to be heard. Ask whether they want to talk or work out a solution together. When shared plans differ, leave room to consider and decline. Deciding together can help the relationship more than deciding quickly.

careers.title: Project coordination
careers.detail: Break a small task into responsibilities and dates. Notice whether you enjoy following through as well as starting.

careers.title: Product experiments
careers.detail: Make a short draft and seek feedback from real users. Notice whether you can revise the plan in response.

careers.title: Operational improvement
careers.detail: Record a bottleneck in repeated work, adjust one step and compare the actual effects.

careers.title: Event delivery
careers.detail: Coordinate the time, budget and arrangements for a small event. Observe communication when plans change.

careers.title: Customer follow-up
careers.detail: Within your authority, clarify a specific request, its owner and response time, then experience following it through.

careers.title: Cross-team collaboration
careers.detail: List handover information and dependencies. Notice whether you understand both sides’ constraints and confirm agreement.

careers.title: Clarifying requirements
careers.detail: Ask for an example of a finished outcome, write the acceptance criteria and check that you understand each other.

careers.title: Organising a small team
careers.detail: Coordinate a voluntary collaboration and notice your reactions to assigning, coordinating and finishing work.

experiment.title: Ask one more question before the next proposal.
experiment.body: Choose an everyday, low-risk discussion. After proposing a plan, invite someone who has not spoken to explain the step that concerns them. Listen before deciding. Record three lines: the original plan, the new information and what changed. If nothing changed, record why.
experiment.phrase: “I have a small plan we could try. Before deciding, which step concerns you most? What would make us pause?”
experiment.review: Review: did the plan change? Was the other person’s concern addressed?

single-i.title: The Communicator
single-i.headline: Turn an idea into a conversation.
single-i.introduction: In this attempt, expression-and-engagement options received your highest count. When an idea is still forming, do you tend to share it first and hear how others respond? This count is not a measure of extraversion or popularity.
portrait: Some ideas become clearer through conversation. Rather than work out every detail alone, you may offer an image, a story or a question so others can participate.

When planning a weekend activity, for example, you might suggest an interesting place and ask what everyone looks forward to. Conversation can draw out previously unspoken interests and unexpected options.

Expression provides material for discussion, but a vivid explanation does not guarantee shared understanding. Notice whether people respond to the idea or the atmosphere. Confirm concrete arrangements when it is time to act.
Notice whether an enthusiastic discussion leads you to agree too quickly. An exciting idea still needs time, resources and a willing owner. Leave room to check before making a commitment.

Alternate expression and listening: pause after one point and invite the other person to add to it or explain their understanding. Recall a time you chose quiet reflection and consider what conditions led to that different approach.

strengths.title: Offer an entry into discussion
strengths.body: Start with a specific story or question so people know what they can respond to, rather than leaving them with an abstract topic.

strengths.title: Make ideas easier to understand
strengths.body: Use examples to explain a proposal, then ask what remains unclear. The value of expression is shared understanding.

strengths.title: Invite more people to participate
strengths.body: Replace a general invitation with a specific question, while leaving a later channel for people who prefer not to answer immediately.

strengths.title: Open up new options
strengths.body: Offer several possibilities before selecting with the group. Make room for choices and for constraints to emerge.

strengths.title: Bring feedback back into the conversation
strengths.body: Explain how a new perspective changed the proposal so participants know their contribution was considered.

edges.title: Confusing a good atmosphere with agreement
edges.body: Before ending, confirm how each person understands the next step. Nods and laughter are not explicit agreement to an arrangement.

edges.title: Talking without room for a reply
edges.body: Make one point at a time, then listen fully. Good communication also lets others decide how they participate.

edges.title: Promising too much when excited
edges.body: Check your time and existing tasks before agreeing. Saying you will confirm later is clearer than failing to deliver.

edges.title: Being driven by a quiet response
edges.body: Someone who does not immediately respond may need time. Ask whether information is missing instead of filling the silence with more words.

work: For discussion, explanation or feedback tasks, prepare an example people can respond to. Afterwards, separate questions, suggestions and confirmed decisions when recording the different views.
For delivery, give promising ideas an owner, scope and date. Check what feedback actually means: rejecting a plan need not mean rejecting you. Look for conditions that can be adjusted.
relationships: Sharing observations and expectations may help you feel connected. Ask whether the other person has energy to talk, and invite their everyday experiences too, so sharing goes both ways.

When views differ, first reflect what matters to them, then explain your perspective. Enthusiasm need not receive an instant response. Hearing “not now” or “let me think” can make the relationship more comfortable.

careers.title: Introducing an event
careers.detail: Write a short invitation and ask whether readers understand the topic and arrangements.

careers.title: User interviews
careers.detail: Prepare open questions and practise listening fully before following up rather than presenting a solution.

careers.title: Explaining content
careers.detail: Use an everyday example to explain a complex concept and ask what is still confusing.

careers.title: Collaborative ideation
careers.detail: Invite different ideas, then choose one to try together.

careers.title: Customer communication
careers.detail: Explain a service and confirm the other person understands its scope and limits.

careers.title: Community organisation
careers.detail: Host a small discussion and notice the kinds of response different participants need.

careers.title: Presenting proposals
careers.detail: Introduce an initial plan and record differences between the audience’s understanding and your intention.

careers.title: Organising feedback
careers.detail: Group suggestions from a discussion and check with participants for misunderstandings.

experiment.title: Leave a pause after your next contribution.
experiment.body: Choose an everyday topic, make one point and ask the other person to explain their understanding. Record what you intended, what they heard and what needed adding.
experiment.phrase: “I’ll pause here. What came through most clearly, and what would you like to ask?”
experiment.review: Review: what did they add? Did it change how you explained the idea?

single-s.title: The Supporter
single-s.headline: Make room for everyone to keep pace.
single-s.introduction: In this attempt, steady-support options received your highest count. Consider whether you first notice who can keep up, whether commitments are sustainable and whether plans fit people’s circumstances. This does not mean you must provide all the care.
portrait: When a task needs ongoing cooperation, you may first ask whether it can last: is the pace workable, is responsibility clear, and who needs support? Steady progress can matter more than doing a lot at once.

When preparing a meal with friends, for example, you might ask what each person can take on and whether the timing works. Such attention brings a plan closer to reality rather than leaving it attractive only on paper.
Steady support can appear in small actions: remembering an agreement, communicating a change or asking why someone has fallen behind. Check whether these examples fit your actual experiences.
Hiding inconvenience to preserve harmony may leave others thinking you always have capacity. Support built on reluctant agreement is difficult to sustain.

Include your conditions in the plan: what you can do, until when, and where someone needs to take over. Recall a time you actively changed a plan. Stability need not mean keeping everything as it was.

strengths.title: Build pace into the plan
strengths.body: Check how much time people can contribute so the arrangement can continue, including space for necessary rest.

strengths.title: Follow through on agreements
strengths.body: Check the progress of what was agreed, and communicate changes promptly to reduce waiting and guesswork.

strengths.title: Notice when someone falls behind
strengths.body: Ask why a response is missing: information may have been missed, time may conflict or responsibility may need changing.

strengths.title: Attend to handover details
strengths.body: Explain what is complete and what remains so the next person knows where to begin.

strengths.title: Give others room to explain
strengths.body: Hear different circumstances before discussing a shared arrangement, without requiring everyone to move at the same pace.

edges.title: Hiding what is inconvenient
edges.body: State your time and energy limits before agreeing. Clear conditions help prevent prolonged reluctant commitments.

edges.title: Letting small problems become burdens
edges.body: Raise one concrete difficulty early instead of waiting to voice accumulated frustration all at once.

edges.title: Automatically filling others’ gaps
edges.body: Check what happened before covering for someone. Even temporary help needs a time for responsibility to return.

edges.title: Keeping an arrangement because it is familiar
edges.body: Ask why a change is needed and what it affects. A small trial can precede accepting or rejecting the whole change.

work: For ongoing cooperation, support the team with clear agreements: record handovers, keep response times predictable and explain resource shortages early. Include your own workload in the arrangement.
When a plan changes, ask for its purpose, transition period and what stays the same. Concrete conditions help find a workable pace more than silent acceptance or general worry.
relationships: You may express care by keeping promises, being present and offering everyday help. Ask which support actually helps, and explain what you want to do and when you need rest.

Discomfort need not become severe before you mention it. Explain a specific situation, your feelings and needs, then adjust the agreement together. Clear boundaries can protect a sustainable relationship.

careers.title: Service follow-up
careers.detail: Follow a small accepted request through and experience ongoing responses and handovers.

careers.title: Event support
careers.detail: Check participants’ time constraints and try a pace they can sustain.

careers.title: Helping newcomers
careers.detail: Explain a process to someone new and ask where more help is needed.

careers.title: Maintaining processes
careers.detail: Record the steps of an everyday task and find handovers that are easily missed.

careers.title: Study companionship
careers.detail: Arrange a review with a study partner and check whether the agreement is manageable for both.

careers.title: Team scheduling
careers.detail: Gather available time from each person before agreeing a small round of work.

careers.title: Organising records
careers.detail: Clarify progress and remaining tasks so others can continue the work.

careers.title: Mapping support resources
careers.detail: List possible support for a small task and confirm providers are willing to help.

experiment.title: State your conditions before the next yes.
experiment.body: Choose an everyday request. Check what you can take on before replying. Record the limits you stated, the response and the final agreement.
experiment.phrase: “I’d like to help with this part and can contribute until Friday. After that, we’ll need to find someone to take over.”
experiment.review: Review: was the agreement clearer? Did it reduce reluctant commitments?

single-c.title: The Checker
single-c.headline: Clarify the evidence and the standard first.
single-c.introduction: In this attempt, standards-and-checking options received your highest count. Before accepting a conclusion or starting a task, do you tend to check evidence, definitions and completion criteria? This count does not measure intelligence or expertise.
portrait: Faced with a promising plan, you may first ask what supports it, what exactly it means and what counts as complete. These questions give discussion something checkable.
When buying a shared item, for example, you might check its dimensions, budget and conditions of use. Clear requirements can prevent discovering different expectations only after the purchase.
Checking may reveal omissions: whether a term has the same meaning to everyone, information has a source or work has acceptance criteria. Judge its value in relation to the actual problem and use.

Checks can keep multiplying without making a decision easier. If essential and minor points are not distinguished, checking can consume delivery time and leave others unsure what is blocking progress.

Before starting, agree which conditions must be checked, what uncertainty can remain and when checking ends. Recall a decision made with incomplete information: which risks needed checking and which could be explored through a small trial?

strengths.title: Align the meaning of words
strengths.body: Replace “soon”, “suitable” and “complete” with concrete conditions to reduce different interpretations of the same words.

strengths.title: Ask where information comes from
strengths.body: Separate confirmed facts, someone’s judgement and unsupported assumptions so decisions rest on clearer information.

strengths.title: Add acceptance criteria
strengths.body: Discuss how delivery will be checked in advance so people know the priorities and avoid repeated revision at the end.

strengths.title: Notice easily missed conditions
strengths.body: Walk through actual use to find interfaces, dimensions or timing that could affect the outcome.

strengths.title: Leave a traceable record
strengths.body: Record the evidence and reasons for a choice. When conditions change, people can see what needs checking again.

edges.title: Giving every detail equal weight
edges.body: Ask what will actually affect the outcome. Separate essentials from later refinements so checking does not continue indefinitely.

edges.title: Waiting for complete certainty
edges.body: For low-risk, reversible tasks, set a checking deadline and use a small trial to fill information gaps.

edges.title: Pointing out a problem without a request
edges.body: Explain which evidence is missing and what would allow work to continue. Concrete conditions are easier to answer than “not rigorous enough”.

edges.title: Replacing conversation with standards
edges.body: Hear why someone faces different constraints. Standards need shared understanding; distinguish requirements from personal preferences.

work: For requirements, checking and delivery tasks, write the key conditions and evidence first, then order checks by risk. When you find a problem, explain its impact and a workable way to address it.
Give checking a time boundary: which conditions allow a start and which need escalation? Explain the purpose to those doing the work so standards support cooperation.
relationships: You may show care by considering arrangements thoroughly and remembering specific needs. Ask what matters most to the other person rather than preparing only to your own standards.

When someone close expresses feelings, they may not need their account checked for accuracy. Confirm that you understand the feeling before checking facts together. Understanding and problem-solving can be separate steps.

careers.title: Verifying information
careers.detail: Find an original source for an explanation and record which claims it directly supports.

careers.title: Organising requirements
careers.detail: Turn a vague request into completion criteria and confirm the intended meaning.

careers.title: Checking delivery
careers.detail: Walk through a small piece of work as a user and distinguish essential from minor issues.

careers.title: Organising data
careers.detail: Check units, missing entries and duplicates in a small table, explaining how you handled them.

careers.title: Explaining a process
careers.detail: Write the inputs and outputs of one step and ask a new user to follow it.

careers.title: Comparing versions
careers.detail: Compare two documents and explain how changes affect users.

careers.title: Testing a sample
careers.detail: Set criteria for a low-risk sample and record what the test finds.

careers.title: Agreeing standards
careers.detail: Agree a delivery standard with a partner and notice how you handle different expectations.

experiment.title: Choose three priorities before the next check.
experiment.body: For a low-risk task, list only the three conditions most important to the outcome and agree when checking will end. Afterwards, record which information changed the decision.
experiment.phrase: “I’d like to confirm these three points before we start. We can try the remaining details and adjust from feedback.”
experiment.review: Review: which checks helped? Which details could have waited until the next step?

tied-d-i.title: D / I tied
tied-d-i.headline: Share the proposal, then confirm the next step.
tied-d-i.introduction: Moving things forward and engaging through expression share the highest count in this attempt. Review proposing action and inviting responses separately. A tie assigns no primary or secondary direction and does not establish two kinds of ability.
portrait: D and I have equal highest counts. Consider when you first propose a next step and when you first open discussion. Equal counts do not explain why either choice occurred.

When organising a weekend trip, you might propose a destination or share interesting plans along the route. One gives discussion a starting point for action; the other invites expectations. Review them separately.
A clear proposal helps others respond, but popularity does not make it executable. As enthusiasm rises, still check the time, budget and who is willing to take on specific work.
Notice a possible gap: everyone talks eagerly, but nobody confirms what happens next. Rather than calling for more enthusiasm, distinguish ideas, agreement and commitments in writing.
Review two different experiences: one about moving forward, one about expression. Record the help and costs of each without combining them into a “charismatic leader” identity.

strengths.title: Make a proposal easy to respond to
strengths.body: Say what you propose, then offer a concrete example so feedback addresses the content rather than only the atmosphere.

strengths.title: Give discussion an action entry point
strengths.body: Choose a small reversible trial from the ideas and ask whether participants want to join.

strengths.title: Invite views that are still unspoken
strengths.body: Pause after proposing and ask those who have not spoken about their conditions, so action uses fuller information.

strengths.title: Distinguish interest from commitment
strengths.body: Confirm “sounds interesting” separately from “I will own this step” so assignments have a clear basis.

strengths.title: Bring new feedback into the plan
strengths.body: Explain which comment changed the proposal and confirm the revised next step with participants.

edges.title: Treating enthusiasm as an execution condition
edges.body: Even in a lively discussion, check resources and time. Interest does not mean someone has capacity for the task.

edges.title: Speaking and deciding too quickly
edges.body: Allow questions and later replies. Do not let the pace of your explanation replace a shared decision.

edges.title: Letting new ideas displace old commitments
edges.body: Before another trial, check whether existing work is complete, handed over or explicitly paused.

edges.title: Hearing disagreement as spoiling the mood
edges.body: Ask which condition concerns the other person. Check the issue before continuing, changing or dropping the proposal.

work: For proposals and task starts, invite feedback through a brief explanation, then turn confirmed parts into a small action. Separate ideas, decisions, owners and dates in meeting notes to prevent different understandings afterwards.
Check communication as well as action: who has not heard about a change, and who has not agreed to a task? Expression and forward action each have costs; choose what this round needs most.
relationships: For shared plans, express expectations and suggest arrangements. Ask how much involvement the other person wants, and leave thinking time for someone without an immediate view.
When opinions differ, separate wanting to try something from requiring everyone to do it. Hear concerns before discussing the next step rather than using enthusiasm to obtain agreement.

careers.title: Proposal discussions
careers.detail: Explain an idea with an example, then ask which part participants would try first.

careers.title: Starting an event
careers.detail: Invite people while checking both interest and actual available time.

careers.title: Product demonstrations
careers.detail: Show a draft and distinguish interest, questions and explicit needs.

careers.title: Requirements conversations
careers.detail: Confirm a shared goal before recording completion criteria for this round.

careers.title: Co-creation workshops
careers.detail: Collect different ideas and choose only one jointly agreed small experiment.

careers.title: Customer follow-up
careers.detail: Explain the next handling step and check acceptance of its scope.

careers.title: Project starts
careers.detail: Turn lively discussion into owners, deliverables and review dates.

careers.title: Reviewing feedback
careers.detail: Record how the plan changed and whether discussion produced useful revisions.

experiment.title: Turn an enthusiastic discussion into one clear agreement.
experiment.body: Choose a low-risk proposal. Invite feedback, then separately confirm who is interested and who will take responsibility. Set only one next step and record unresolved conditions.
experiment.phrase: “Which part would you be willing to try first? Please also say if now is not convenient.”
experiment.review: Review: were interest and commitment distinct? Does the next step have a clear owner?

tied-d-s.title: D / S tied
tied-d-s.headline: Offer a next step and time to adjust.
tied-d-s.introduction: Moving things forward and steady support share the highest count. Review starting tasks and considering pace in separate situations. A tie does not establish that you always combine speed with support or identify one as more representative of you.
portrait: D and S share the highest count. Ask separately how you get something started and how you check that people can continue. Equal counts may come from entirely different situations.

When moving home together, for example, you might list today’s tasks or ask until when each helper is available. Starting and supporting solve different problems and need not occur in the same action.
A next step still needs a pace people can sustain. Clarifying workload and time lets participants judge whether they want to accept the arrangement.
Pushing for a start while filling every gap may increase your own burden. Support need not mean taking on all remaining work.
Recall a time you pushed for change and one when you kept an arrangement. Consider the goals, limits and participants’ needs rather than describing the tie as an innate balancing ability.

strengths.title: Discuss progress and workload together
strengths.body: Explain the intended outcome and ask about available time so the plan can be jointly confirmed.

strengths.title: Start change on a small scale
strengths.body: Try it for a limited time while keeping familiar support, giving people a chance to explain its effects.

strengths.title: Arrange a clear handover
strengths.body: Confirm who follows up and what information and preparation time the recipient needs.

strengths.title: Notice difficulty taking work on
strengths.body: Ask why progress stopped before negotiating smaller scope, more resources or different timing.

strengths.title: Leave a review point for ongoing work
strengths.body: Schedule a workload review as well as a start, and address reluctantly accepted commitments early.

edges.title: Planning faster than people can adjust
edges.body: Explain the purpose and transition, and check understanding rather than only asking whether people can begin immediately.

edges.title: Taking on every team gap
edges.body: Confirm responsibility and an end date before covering. Bring genuine resource shortages back for shared discussion.

edges.title: Delaying concerns to preserve harmony
edges.body: Use a concrete fact to raise difficulty early rather than waiting until the deadline to say you cannot continue.

edges.title: Making incompatible promises
edges.body: If promising both speed and every requested accommodation, check whether available resources can support both.

work: When proposing a change, explain its purpose, first step and transition period together. Ask participants to state what they can take on before assigning responsibility and a review date.
If progress conflicts with workload, make trade-offs visible: reduce scope, reorder work or adjust the deadline. Do not sustain an unworkable plan only by filling gaps yourself.
relationships: For shared plans, state both your hopes and your capacity. If the other person needs a slower pace, ask how much time or information is needed, then agree a small step.
Caring need not mean always yielding. Explain inconvenience early and allow the other person to decline. Willingly accepted commitments are more sustainable than apparent smoothness.

careers.title: Coordinating change
careers.detail: Explain a small change’s purpose and ask what transition people need.

careers.title: Project scheduling
careers.detail: Compare tasks with available time and agree a manageable first round.

careers.title: Event delivery
careers.detail: Set a next step while leaving room for rest, handovers and changes.

careers.title: Service improvement
careers.detail: Trial a process and ask those using it about workload and pace.

careers.title: Team handovers
careers.detail: Confirm timing and preparation needs, noticing forced last-minute cover.

careers.title: Community cooperation
careers.detail: Arrange voluntary responsibilities and follow-up for a small task.

careers.title: Ongoing follow-up
careers.detail: Check progress and whether the original arrangement still fits.

careers.title: Finishing tasks
careers.detail: Check who owns remaining work so it does not all fall to one person.

experiment.title: Set a next step and ask what people can take on.
experiment.body: For a small collaboration, separately record the goal, each person’s available time and a review point. Negotiate scope before automatically filling any gap yourself.
experiment.phrase: “Let’s complete this small step first. With the time you have, which part can you take on and what needs adjusting?”
experiment.review: Review: did anyone agree reluctantly? Were progress and workload both discussed?

tied-d-c.title: D / C tied
tied-d-c.headline: Give forward action clear completion criteria.
tied-d-c.introduction: Moving things forward and standards and checks share the highest count. Consider separately when you act first and when you check first. A tie establishes neither more accurate decisions nor an ability to be both efficient and rigorous.
portrait: D and C share this attempt’s highest count. Ask why you wanted to start promptly and what needed checking first. Equal counts do not show equal skill in using either approach.

For a shared presentation, you might set a draft deadline or confirm data sources and delivery requirements beforehand. Action points and checking conditions can be discussed together, but each needs evidence.
Putting the intended task and its completion criteria in one agreement helps align expectations. Disagreement can then be identified as a question of goals, methods or standards.
Requiring speed while continually adding checks may leave people unsure when they can deliver. State essential conditions early and discuss the cost of new requirements.

Choose a low-risk, adjustable task, confirm necessary conditions and arrange a small trial. Review which checks changed the plan and which details could wait. Every attempt need not be fast and perfect.

strengths.title: Connect goals and acceptance
strengths.body: When setting the next step, say what counts as complete so the task has a clear start and finish.

strengths.title: Find the actual blocking condition
strengths.body: Ask which missing information prevents progress and prioritise that gap instead of expanding every question.

strengths.title: Use small trials to gather evidence
strengths.body: For reversible decisions, test a limited scope and use feedback to decide whether to continue.

strengths.title: Give disagreement a concrete subject
strengths.body: Distinguish facts, assumptions and personal expectations so different views address the same issue.

strengths.title: Keep the reasons for decisions
strengths.body: Record why this step was chosen and what is unconfirmed so later revisions do not require guesswork.

edges.title: Demanding speed while adding standards
edges.body: If a new check affects progress, explain why and renegotiate delivery scope or timing.

edges.title: Using checking instead of trying
edges.body: Distinguish reversible decisions from high-risk ones. Set a checking limit for low-risk tasks, then learn through a trial.

edges.title: Treating different methods as inadequate
edges.body: Check the agreed essentials, allow different approaches and distinguish standards from preferences.

edges.title: Using urgency to skip conditions
edges.body: Even under pressure, confirm safety, authority and mandatory requirements. Progress alone does not justify omissions.

work: Before starting, record the goal, acceptance criteria and review time together. Order checks by risk: usability and safety first, refinements afterwards.

When something does not meet conditions, explain the gap, impact and possible corrections. Renegotiate scope when requirements change rather than keeping the original deadline alongside growing demands.
relationships: For shared plans, propose arrangements and explain the conditions you care about. If the other person chooses another method, ask whether it still meets shared needs rather than judging it against your process.
In disagreement, distinguish feelings and facts. When understanding is needed, listen before discussing details and action, so the relationship is not an inspection that must produce a verdict.

careers.title: Prototype validation
careers.detail: Make a low-risk draft with conditions to test and a stopping point set in advance.

careers.title: Delivery coordination
careers.detail: Confirm the next delivery’s scope and acceptance criteria together.

careers.title: Process improvement
careers.detail: Adjust one step and record before-and-after data and user feedback.

careers.title: Confirming requirements
careers.detail: Turn a request into observable completion criteria and check shared understanding.

careers.title: Investigating problems
careers.detail: List facts and hypotheses, checking only the most important one first.

careers.title: Test coordination
careers.detail: Order checks and separate mandatory passes from later refinements.

careers.title: Recording changes
careers.detail: Record how a new requirement affects time, scope and responsibility.

careers.title: Project reviews
careers.detail: Identify evidence that changed a decision and checks that did not help.

experiment.title: Give the next step three completion criteria.
experiment.body: For a small adjustable task, list only three essential conditions and agree a checking time. Afterwards, record new requirements and their actual benefits.
experiment.phrase: “This round will cover these three points. We’ll record other details and decide after reviewing whether to add them.”
experiment.review: Review: were conditions clear in advance? Did checking displace finishing the task?

tied-i-s.title: I / S tied
tied-i-s.headline: Invite responses and make room for different paces.
tied-i-s.introduction: Engaging through expression and steady support share the highest count. Review sharing ideas and considering cooperation separately. This does not establish that you always understand others or must manage everyone’s emotions.
portrait: I and S share the highest count. Consider how you invite conversation and how you make communication sustainable. Equal counts do not mean you always do both in every setting.
When planning a gathering, you may suggest an interesting activity or first ask whether everyone has energy to attend. One concerns expression and participation, the other pace and capacity.
Listening can give new ideas a hearing, but preserving atmosphere does not require unanimous answers. Someone who does not want to participate should also be able to say so clearly.
Wanting everyone to be happy while hiding your limits may leave a real burden beneath apparent harmony. Support in a relationship should include your needs too.
Compare a conversation that felt fulfilling with one that felt draining. Consider differences in topic, pace, responsibility and willingness, rather than explaining them only through a type.

strengths.title: Offer different ways to respond
strengths.body: Invite discussion now or a message later, so participation does not depend only on immediate expression.

strengths.title: Ask about capacity first
strengths.body: Before sharing or asking for help, check whether the other person is available so both willingly enter the exchange.

strengths.title: Consider interest and workload together
strengths.body: When people like an idea, also discuss available time to prevent enthusiasm becoming reluctant work.

strengths.title: Make space for quiet views
strengths.body: Notice who has not spoken, offer a private invitation and accept that they may not want to join yet.

strengths.title: Keep checking whether support helps
strengths.body: Arrange a brief review of useful support and what should be reduced or changed.

edges.title: Assuming harmony means no disagreement
edges.body: Ask specific questions about differing views rather than inferring satisfaction from the atmosphere.

edges.title: Exhausting yourself through companionship
edges.body: State your available time beforehand and allow yourself to rest afterwards. Continuous responsiveness is not required.

edges.title: Guessing what someone needs
edges.body: Ask whether they want listening, advice or practical help instead of treating your good intentions as their answer.

edges.title: Avoiding interruption of an unsuitable arrangement
edges.body: Propose a small change when uncomfortable, giving both people a chance to adjust before continuing becomes impossible.

work: For discussions, explain the issue and offer both immediate and later feedback channels. Check different views at the end instead of treating quietness or nods as agreement.
Agree scope and an end time before supporting someone. Helping them find resources does not automatically make you responsible for subsequent execution; confirm that assignment separately.
relationships: Sharing daily experiences and sustained presence can support connection; ask how the other person likes to communicate. Negotiate frequency and response speed rather than using quick replies to measure care.
Ask what an upset person needs, and state when you are tired too. Both being able to express limits helps care continue without one person constantly giving.

careers.title: Group conversations
careers.detail: Use open questions and quiet thinking time, observing how people respond.

careers.title: Service communication
careers.detail: Confirm needed help and explain what you can provide.

careers.title: Newcomer support
careers.detail: Invite questions and check whether the information is manageable.

careers.title: Organising learning
careers.detail: Agree discussion frequency with a partner and experience the cost of sustained participation.

careers.title: Community activities
careers.detail: Let members choose their involvement rather than requiring visible activity from everyone.

careers.title: Collecting feedback
careers.detail: Offer private comments and check their meaning is understood accurately.

careers.title: Team support
careers.detail: Ask what support is needed and whether the provider has capacity.

careers.title: Reviewing collaboration
careers.detail: Discuss communication in a collaboration and identify interruptions to reduce.

experiment.title: Ask what kind of company is wanted before the next conversation.
experiment.body: For an everyday exchange, ask whether the other person wants listening, joint problem-solving or rest. State your available time too and record how it felt afterwards.
experiment.phrase: “Is now a good time to talk? Would you like me to listen first or think through options with you?”
experiment.review: Review: were needs clarified? Could both people end the conversation and rest?

tied-i-c.title: I / C tied
tied-i-c.headline: Give an idea a clear picture and a basis to check.
tied-i-c.introduction: Engaging through expression and standards and checks share the highest count. Consider explaining ideas and checking evidence separately. A tie does not establish more persuasive expression or more reliable conclusions.
portrait: I and C share the highest count, offering separate questions about expression and checking. Equal counts do not show that you always research before speaking or establish a combined identity.

When recommending an item to a friend, you may share your experience or check specifications and use conditions. Experience and facts serve different purposes; let listeners know which you are discussing.
Concrete examples help people understand ideas, while sources let them check facts. Observe how these connect in an actual explanation.
A fluent story may make unconfirmed parts sound factual. Conversely, explaining every detail may hide the main point from the listener.
Try giving the conclusion and key evidence first, noting uncertainty and inviting questions. Record which explanations helped understanding and which checks changed the judgement.

strengths.title: Make abstract content concrete
strengths.body: Choose an example relevant to the listener’s experience and say what it cannot represent.

strengths.title: Distinguish experience from fact
strengths.body: Identify personal impressions and checkable sources so the other person can judge for themselves.

strengths.title: Make questions discussable
strengths.body: Ask what the listener most wants verified, then provide relevant evidence rather than every available document.

strengths.title: Revise explanations through feedback
strengths.body: When understanding differs from your intention, check the example, definition and evidence for gaps.

strengths.title: Leave sources for key conclusions
strengths.body: Add original sources after a short explanation for people who want to investigate further.

edges.title: Letting the story exceed the evidence
edges.body: Clearly identify unconfirmed speculation. A vivid explanation cannot replace missing support.

edges.title: Providing information without a clear thread
edges.body: Ask what the listener needs to resolve, give two or three relevant points and leave the rest as supporting material.

edges.title: Selecting evidence to persuade
edges.body: Check information that challenges the proposal too, and explain limits and alternative interpretations.

edges.title: Polishing endlessly before speaking
edges.body: For a low-risk discussion, explain the current version and unconfirmed parts, then develop it through feedback.

work: For explanations and proposals, separate the problem, key evidence and unresolved conditions. Establish what is being discussed, then invite feedback on facts or the plan.
Keep reasons for revision: new evidence, misunderstanding or changed goals. Do not hide uncertainty to improve presentation or let details bury the central issue.
relationships: When sharing information, distinguish personal experience from verified facts. If views differ, ask what experiences inform them rather than turning conversation into an argument.
Understand a feeling before checking facts. Right and wrong may not be the issue this exchange needs to resolve; ask what response the other person wants.

careers.title: Explaining knowledge
careers.detail: Use an everyday example to explain a concept and identify its main evidence.

careers.title: Presenting information
careers.detail: Organise information into three points and ask readers to explain their understanding.

careers.title: Proposal communication
careers.detail: State suggestions and assumptions, inviting the conditions listeners most want checked.

careers.title: Content checking
careers.detail: Check whether an explanation presents personal experience as a general fact.

careers.title: User education
careers.detail: Use questions to decide whether to add an example or a definition.

careers.title: Organising interviews
careers.detail: Distinguish quotations, interpretations and speculation; confirm important wording with the interviewee.

careers.title: Comparing information
careers.detail: Compare two sources’ evidence and scope, then explain differences clearly.

careers.title: Reviewing presentations
careers.detail: Record misunderstandings and check whether structure or evidence needs revision.

experiment.title: Separate facts and ideas in one explanation.
experiment.body: Choose information to share and mark verified facts, personal experiences and unconfirmed speculation. Explain it in two minutes and ask what the other person most wants to explore.
experiment.phrase: “This is the evidence I found, and this is my idea. Which part would you most like to check first?”
experiment.review: Review: could the listener distinguish fact and speculation? Did the explanation exceed its evidence?

tied-s-c.title: S / C tied
tied-s-c.headline: Turn dependability into clear agreements.
tied-s-c.introduction: Steady support and standards and checks share the highest count. Review ongoing cooperation and confirming standards separately. A tie does not mean you must cover every gap or establish that you are more dependable than others.
portrait: S and C share the highest count. Ask separately whether an arrangement can continue and whether its conditions are clear. They may be chosen in different situations rather than represent a measured combined ability.
When caring for a shared plant, you might ask who has time to water it or confirm watering and light requirements. Ongoing support and checking conditions address different difficulties.
Written everyday agreements can reduce repeated explanations. A clear process still needs realistic workload, and willingness to cooperate is not a reason to keep adding demands.
Continual checking and covering to maintain stability may leave you carrying unspoken responsibilities. Support and quality should not depend only on one person’s quiet maintenance.
Recall a time you changed an old process and why it mattered. Agreements can be renegotiated, and uncertainty can be recorded honestly.

strengths.title: Write everyday agreements clearly
strengths.body: State frequency, scope and completion criteria so people know how to cooperate and when to hand over.

strengths.title: Make handovers easy to continue
strengths.body: Leave progress, problems and necessary evidence so the next person can decide where to begin.

strengths.title: Check actual capacity
strengths.body: After setting standards, ask whether available time and resources support them, avoiding prolonged burdens.

strengths.title: Notice repeated problems
strengths.body: Record the conditions behind recurring omissions and discuss process changes rather than repeatedly repairing them.

strengths.title: Give change a transition
strengths.body: Explain why a rule changes, what differs and when it starts, leaving preparation and question time.

edges.title: Quietly becoming the final backup
edges.body: Explain who needs to address a gap and the scope and end time of any help you provide this time.

edges.title: Making old processes harder to change
edges.body: Regularly ask what a step still solves, allowing checks without a purpose to be removed.

edges.title: Avoiding saying a standard is unmanageable
edges.body: State the gap between resources and requirements and negotiate scope instead of hiding it through prolonged overtime.

edges.title: Letting detailed reminders become resentment
edges.body: Explain an omission and its effect early and confirm a correction rather than saving everything until frustration grows.

work: For process maintenance or handovers, put essential steps, owners and completion conditions in one explanation. Ask actual users to try it and confirm that it is clear and manageable.
Discuss recurring gaps as team responsibilities and resources rather than automatically accepting them as your job. Once a process is stable, set a review of whether its steps are still needed.
relationships: In shared living, clear agreements reduce guesswork: who does what, to what standard and what happens if they cannot. Ask which rules express a need and which are simply habits.

Propose changes directly when an agreement does not fit. Understand the other person’s circumstances and explain your workload. One person need not keep reminding and cleaning up to support the relationship.

careers.title: Handover explanations
careers.detail: Write progress and remaining tasks clearly, then ask the recipient to use the notes.

careers.title: Process maintenance
careers.detail: Check whether familiar steps remain useful and identify simplifications.

careers.title: Service records
careers.detail: Organise a request’s handling so later follow-up can see the basis.

careers.title: Checking schedules
careers.detail: Compare completion standards and available time to discuss adjustments.

careers.title: Archiving materials
careers.detail: Organise versions and purposes, asking users whether they can find what they need.

careers.title: Routine checks
careers.detail: List essential checks for a low-risk task and agree who addresses problems.

careers.title: Updating rules
careers.detail: Explain a small change and collect difficulties from those implementing it.

careers.title: Reviewing recurring issues
careers.detail: Record conditions behind a repeated omission and discuss process, not only blame.

experiment.title: Clarify one agreement that has become assumed.
experiment.body: Choose a task where you often cover a gap. Write the original division, completion criteria and actual workload. Agree who owns the next round and how to hand over if unavailable.
experiment.phrase: “Let’s agree this again: which part does each of us own, and how will we tell the other if we cannot do it?”
experiment.review: Review: is responsibility clearer? Is the original standard necessary?

tied-d-i-s.title: D / I / S tied
tied-d-i-s.headline: Give action, expression and support their own place.
tied-d-i-s.introduction: Moving things forward, engaging through expression and steady support share the highest count. Review starting, communicating and sustaining cooperation separately. A tie does not show you can combine all three; selecting C less often does not mean lacking checking ability.
portrait: D, I and S have equal highest counts. They offer three separate questions: how to begin, invite responses and sustain cooperation. They are not a new three-letter personality.
When preparing a meal with friends, you might set a next step, invite ideas or check what everyone can take on. Review what you actually did first and why you chose it.
An enthusiastic discussion and a plan still need completion criteria. C, though outside the highest tie, remains a useful perspective for checking arrangements.
Wanting quick progress, everyone’s satisfaction and responsibility for all remaining work can create incompatible promises. State trade-offs rather than filling every gap alone.
Record action, expression and support separately in one collaboration, considering what helped and what needs adjusting. You need not use all three approaches in every task.

strengths.title: Confirm starting and joining separately
strengths.body: After proposing a first step, ask whether others understand and what they want to join. A proposal does not automatically assign work.

strengths.title: Let ideas meet real conditions
strengths.body: Gather time and energy limits while discussing possibilities to identify a manageable scope for this round.

strengths.title: Leave a review point for cooperation
strengths.body: After starting, check the pace again and allow participants to adjust commitments to actual workload.

strengths.title: Accept different forms of response
strengths.body: Listen to ideas in the room and leave a later opportunity for quieter people to contribute.

strengths.title: Keep a clear record for the next round
strengths.body: Record decisions, responsibilities and unresolved questions so cooperation does not rely only on the discussion’s atmosphere.

edges.title: Trying to satisfy everyone
edges.body: Conflicting needs require shared trade-offs; continually expanding your own responsibility is not the only answer.

edges.title: Enthusiasm without completion criteria
edges.body: Confirm what counts as done before starting. A smooth discussion does not establish a clear goal.

edges.title: Coordinating while overlooking your workload
edges.body: Include your time in the plan and explain early what needs someone else to take over.

edges.title: Changing faster than people can adjust
edges.body: Change one important part at a time, explain why and hear the practical difficulties it creates.

work: At the start of a collaboration, separately confirm the goal, willingness to join and manageable scope. Agree a small round of work, then use clear review points for progress and workload feedback.
Record disagreement and add acceptance criteria. Expression, action and support each serve a purpose; three counts should not assign roles to you or colleagues.
relationships: Shared activities can include both hopes and choice: suggest something, hear the other person’s view and confirm what each can contribute. Taking initiative does not require the other person to comply.

If preserving harmony leads to excessive responsibility, state difficulty early. Changing a plan, reducing activity or resting can also be good interaction, rather than keeping every original proposal.

careers.title: Event preparation
careers.detail: Confirm the goal, willingness to attend and what each person can take on separately.

careers.title: Team starts
careers.detail: Turn discussion into small tasks while recording matters not yet agreed.

careers.title: Study groups
careers.detail: Invite topic choices and agree a sustainable discussion frequency.

careers.title: Service coordination
careers.detail: Collect requests and resource limits before promising a response for this round.

careers.title: Community co-creation
careers.detail: Invite ideas and allow members to join only a small part.

careers.title: Communication reviews
careers.detail: Check whether decisions were understood and assignments explicitly accepted.

careers.title: Scheduling tasks
careers.detail: Compare plans with actual workload and discuss what to reduce.

careers.title: Delivery explanations
careers.detail: Add completion criteria and check whether those doing the task know how to finish.

experiment.title: Confirm three things separately in one collaboration.
experiment.body: For a small task, ask what to do, who wants to join and how much time is available. Add a completion condition and record the scope everyone accepts.
experiment.phrase: “Let’s clarify the goal and hear everyone’s ideas. With the time available, what can this round reasonably cover?”
experiment.review: Review: can commitments be kept? Did unspoken views get treated as agreement?

tied-d-i-c.title: D / I / C tied
tied-d-i-c.headline: Turn a proposal into a small, checkable step.
tied-d-i-c.introduction: Moving things forward, engaging through expression and standards and checks share the highest count. Review action, communication and evidence separately. This does not establish a more reliable proposal; selecting S less often does not mean lacking care or follow-through.
portrait: D, I and C share the highest count. They offer perspectives on starting, discussing and checking, not evidence of an inherently complete problem-solving process.
For a small exhibition, you might explain an idea, propose a trial or check display requirements. Distinguish what actually happened in experience from what you selected in these questions.
A clear proposal with defined conditions still needs people with time to execute it. S being outside the highest tie does not prevent you from asking about pace and workload.
Quick proposals, extensive explanations and rising standards can leave colleagues unsure what to answer first. Order the questions instead of advancing every requirement at once.
Start a small reversible trial: explain the purpose, confirm essentials and ask whether participants can take it on. Record the outcome without assigning a higher ability level to three tied counts.

strengths.title: Give a proposal a discussable structure
strengths.body: Separate purpose, examples and evidence so feedback can address a specific part.

strengths.title: Reduce the next step to a testable scope
strengths.body: Try only the small step that provides key information rather than expanding an early idea into a complete plan.

strengths.title: Make conditions visible early
strengths.body: Include important limits in the explanation so others can decide whether they understand and want to join.

strengths.title: Turn challenges into questions to check
strengths.body: Ask which fact or condition needs verification after hearing disagreement, then decide how to fill the gap.

strengths.title: Revise explanations with evidence
strengths.body: When checking does not support the original idea, explain the change promptly instead of promoting action with the old account.

edges.title: Making too many demands to answer
edges.body: Confirm one key question at a time, separating feedback, standards discussion and action decisions.

edges.title: A complete proposal with nobody available
edges.body: Ask explicitly about resources and workload. Plan quality does not replace execution capacity.

edges.title: Explaining more to defend the original view
edges.body: Make room for contrary evidence and reduce, pause or abandon the trial when needed.

edges.title: Changing standards without changing time
edges.body: Renegotiate scope and deadlines when adding requirements rather than assuming others can absorb every change.

work: Organise a small trial in a one-page explanation: purpose, current evidence, the question to test and the first step. Ask participants to confirm understanding, completion criteria and available time separately.
During review, distinguish clear communication, completion of the trial and evidence supporting the initial idea. They may have different answers and need separate responses.
relationships: For shared plans, explain reasons and hopes while inviting the other person’s conditions. Even a complete explanation still needs a question about willingness and current capacity.
Allow disagreement to remain unresolved for a while. Feelings need not be corrected with more arguments. Ask whether listening or discussing solutions is needed now.

careers.title: Experiment proposals
careers.detail: State purpose and assumptions, then gather evidence through a small trial.

careers.title: Prototype presentations
careers.detail: Explain a draft to users and record misunderstandings and actual needs.

careers.title: Reviewing requirements
careers.detail: Turn feedback into checkable conditions while preserving differing views.

careers.title: Explaining data
careers.detail: Present a finding clearly with its scope and uncertainty.

careers.title: Delivery coordination
careers.detail: Check standards, time and the actual workload people can take on.

careers.title: Process trials
careers.detail: Change one part and consider implementation feedback before wider use.

careers.title: Revising proposals
careers.detail: Revise an idea in light of contrary evidence, explaining changed judgements.

careers.title: Experiment reviews
careers.detail: Check communication, action and evidence separately rather than reducing them to one success verdict.

experiment.title: Reduce one proposal to a single testable question.
experiment.body: For a low-risk idea, write only the issue, existing evidence and one small trial. Invite questions and confirm participants have time before starting.
experiment.phrase: “This round aims to clarify just this point. We’ll start only if the conditions and available time work.”
experiment.review: Review: did the trial answer the question? Was the participants’ workload overlooked?

tied-d-s-c.title: D / S / C tied
tied-d-s-c.headline: Plan the next step around manageable conditions.
tied-d-s-c.introduction: Moving things forward, steady support and standards and checks share the highest count. Review starting, pace and standards separately. A tie does not establish all three abilities; selecting I less often does not mean poor expression.
portrait: D, S and C have equal highest counts. Review how you set a first step, sustain cooperation and check completion conditions separately, rather than combining them into a manager’s profile.
When organising a shared storage space, you might choose today’s scope, ask how long people can help and agree sorting rules. These questions have different purposes and may involve trade-offs.
Even a detailed arrangement needs to be understood. I, though outside the highest tie, can remind you to explain reasons and changes instead of preparing silently.

To meet both deadlines and standards, increasing your own workload may seem like an option. First check whether tasks, resources and requirements can coexist rather than treating personal cover as the only solution.
Use a small task to check whether standards are necessary, pace is sustainable and the next step is clear. Three counts do not require you to take on three people’s responsibilities.

strengths.title: Set scope and workload together
strengths.body: Choose this round’s work and check time and resources rather than compressing the full ideal into the plan.

strengths.title: Make completion criteria workable
strengths.body: Clear standards also need confirmation from those doing the work that they can meet them.

strengths.title: Prepare evidence for handovers
strengths.body: Leave progress, rules and unresolved issues so continuing work does not rely on verbal guesswork.

strengths.title: Clarify what stays the same during change
strengths.body: Explain what changed and what remains so people can judge how to prepare.

strengths.title: Raise workload concerns early
strengths.body: When progress starts displacing rest or quality, discuss scope rather than waiting until delivery for a rescue.

edges.title: Preparing thoroughly without explaining why
edges.body: Explain the plan and invite people to restate their understanding. A document alone does not complete communication.

edges.title: Personally covering every requirement
edges.body: Discuss trade-offs when resources fall short rather than accepting every gap as your permanent responsibility.

edges.title: Never updating a stable process
edges.body: Set a review of whether the original standard still helps and which steps can be reduced.

edges.title: Ignoring real difficulty to meet progress targets
edges.body: Distinguish temporary delay from unworkable conditions and adjust deadlines rather than only increasing pressure.

work: When arranging tasks, record scope, completion conditions, owners and available time together. Ask those doing the work to confirm and leave a route to challenge unrealistic requirements.
For delays, check conditions and resources first. Explain changes and their effects instead of demanding stable execution while adding unexplained standards.
relationships: Everyday agreements can specify scope and frequency while allowing changes. Explain why a condition matters to you and ask about the other person’s needs.
Being dependable does not mean never asking for anything. Explain your workload while offering care and renegotiate inconvenience rather than silently doing everything to prove you care.

careers.title: Small-project scheduling
careers.detail: Bring scope, completion conditions and each person’s available time together.

careers.title: Handover coordination
careers.detail: Organise rules and remaining work, then ask recipients if they can continue.

careers.title: Process pilots
careers.detail: Trial steps on a small scale, collecting workload and outcome feedback.

careers.title: Quality coordination
careers.detail: Distinguish essentials and refinements and confirm resource gaps with those doing the work.

careers.title: Service arrangements
careers.detail: Explain scope, response time and handover when a request falls outside scope.

careers.title: Reducing task burden
careers.detail: Review repeated work and suggest steps to remove or combine.

careers.title: Explaining changes
careers.detail: Clarify differences and ask participants what makes adjustment difficult.

careers.title: Completion reviews
careers.detail: Check who carries remaining tasks so one final person does not cover indefinitely.

experiment.title: Explain a thorough plan to those who will carry it out.
experiment.body: For a small task, write scope, standards and available time. Ask participants what is unclear or unmanageable and revise once in response.
experiment.phrase: “Which step is unclear, and which requirement cannot be met with the time we have? Let’s adjust those first.”
experiment.review: Review: was the plan understood? Did personal cover hide a resource shortage?

tied-i-s-c.title: I / S / C tied
tied-i-s-c.headline: Confirm understanding, pace and accuracy separately.
tied-i-s-c.introduction: Engaging through expression, steady support and standards and checks share the highest count. Review communication, cooperation and checking separately. A tie does not establish that you automatically combine them; selecting D less often does not mean lacking initiative.
portrait: I, S and C share the highest count, inviting separate reviews of explaining ideas, considering pace and checking evidence. Equal counts do not show that these approaches always occur together.
For a reading discussion, you might invite impressions, check everyone’s availability and define the material and topic. Expression, support and checking each address a different issue.
Clear information and a comfortable atmosphere do not settle the next step. D, though outside the highest tie, can still remind you to identify who follows up and when to review.
Repeatedly adding information and accommodating every view may make discussion hard to end. Separate what this round must decide from questions that can remain open.

Review an actual collaboration: what people understood, what they could take on and whether evidence was clear. Record who confirmed the next step rather than inferring natural coordination from the counts.

strengths.title: Make explanations fit the user
strengths.body: Ask what the other person needs to resolve before choosing examples and material, reducing irrelevant information.

strengths.title: Make questions comfortable to ask
strengths.body: Allow people to say they do not understand or are unavailable, checking why instead of treating questions as non-cooperation.

strengths.title: Check how an agreement is understood
strengths.body: Invite participants to explain the next step in their own words and uncover different expectations behind the same term.

strengths.title: Connect evidence with actual circumstances
strengths.body: Explain when evidence applies and hear practical limits from those doing the work.

strengths.title: Record ongoing cooperation
strengths.body: Separate confirmed points from pending issues so work can continue later.

edges.title: Thorough discussion without an end point
edges.body: Agree the question and deadline in advance, record open issues and set a next step.

edges.title: Adding information for fear of omission
edges.body: Check which information is most needed and add only what is relevant to the current decision.

edges.title: Delaying feedback to protect feelings
edges.body: Explain a specific fact and impact promptly, leaving the other person room to explain and revise.

edges.title: Accommodating everyone except yourself
edges.body: Include your time and needs in the agreement instead of assuming continuous explanation and support are your responsibility.

work: For explanations, training or collaborative support, understand the audience’s background and needs first. Explain key information, conditions and feedback channels, then ask actual users whether they can follow.
When discussion ends, identify the owner, timing and pending questions. Check information and pace without requiring everyone’s complete satisfaction before agreeing a small adjustable step.
relationships: Share ideas and ask whether the other person has energy to continue. For shared living arrangements, explain conditions that matter and invite their habits and limits.
In disagreement, confirm feelings, then facts, then a next step. Separating the three can reduce pressure for one conversation to resolve everything.

careers.title: Learning explanations
careers.detail: Understand the listener’s background, explain with an example and collect questions.

careers.title: Service support
careers.detail: Confirm actual needs before explaining conditions and follow-up.

careers.title: Organising material
careers.detail: Arrange information for users and check whether it is easy to find and understand.

careers.title: Collaboration records
careers.detail: Separate agreement and pending issues, then confirm the owner and time.

careers.title: Feedback interviews
careers.detail: Hear the experience fully before checking its specific context.

careers.title: Process training
careers.detail: Ask a new user to try one step and compare explanation with actual use.

careers.title: Team communication
careers.detail: Offer different response methods and set an end point for the discussion.

careers.title: Content trial reading
careers.detail: Ask readers what is unclear and add according to need rather than length.

experiment.title: End a thorough discussion with one clear small step.
experiment.body: For everyday cooperation, confirm shared understanding and conditions, then set one next step, one owner and one review time. Record open questions separately.
experiment.phrase: “What is clear so far? Let’s agree this small step and return to the other questions at the review.”
experiment.review: Review: did discussion have an end point? Did someone explicitly accept the next step?

tied-d-i-s-c.title: D / I / S / C tied
tied-d-i-s-c.headline: Equal counts: return to specific choices.
tied-d-i-s-c.introduction: All four directions received 6 selections and share the highest count. Equal counts within this question set do not mean all-round ability, ideal balance or flexible switching between four styles. No primary direction needs to be selected.
portrait: Equal counts leave no single highest direction for now. The useful question is not which type you really are, but which conditions led you to different approaches in different situations.
For a shared trip, you might sometimes set a next step, discuss expectations, consider whether everyone can keep pace or check the budget. What you actually did needs checking against experience.
Each count of 6 means only that four categories of option were selected equally often here. It does not compare skill or establish that you will cover every consideration in important situations.
You need not find a grander name for this result or ask someone to choose a primary type to resolve uncertainty. Start with a small event and gradually understand your trade-offs.

Record the goal, limits, first action and outcome, then find a counterexample using a different approach. You can leave the conclusion open. This report offers observation questions rather than defining your identity.

strengths.title: Observe the four approaches separately
strengths.body: Turn action, expression, support and checking into separate questions answered through experience, without assigning ability labels first.

strengths.title: Start with what the task needs
strengths.body: Ask whether action, understanding, cooperation or evidence is currently missing, then choose a step to try.

strengths.title: Preserve differences between experiences
strengths.body: Allow different approaches in different settings and record changing conditions rather than forcing one consistent story.

strengths.title: Ask for specific feedback
strengths.body: Invite an example of a behaviour and its impact in an actual collaboration rather than asking what type someone thinks you are.

strengths.title: Leave judgement for further observation
strengths.body: When one record is insufficient, keep the question open. Equal counts alone establish neither strengths nor deficits.

edges.title: Treating equal counts as all-round ability
edges.body: Check skills, experience and feedback separately. Equal selection counts provide no proof of ability.

edges.title: Repeatedly choosing a primary type to settle identity
edges.body: Return to a recent small event: what needed resolving and what did you actually do first?

edges.title: Delaying because any approach seems possible
edges.body: For a low-risk task, choose a small adjustable step and use feedback without waiting for a fixed style.

edges.title: Explaining every change through a label
edges.body: Also record time pressure, role requirements and resources to see whether behaviour changed with real conditions.

work: When receiving a task, you can check the goal, shared understanding, manageable scope and acceptance evidence in turn. This is an optional checklist, not proof from counts that you automatically do all four well.
Assign work according to actual willingness, experience and performance. Take one clearly scoped small task and notice difficulties in starting, communicating, following through and checking.
relationships: Ask directly what the other person wants this time: action together, ideas, quiet company or help organising information. A four-way tie should not decide either person’s needs.
When shared plans differ, state hopes, limits and willing contributions separately. It is fine to agree a later discussion when uncertain instead of presenting yourself as endlessly adaptable.

careers.title: Observing a task start
careers.detail: Choose a small task and record how you set its goal and first step.

careers.title: Observing expression
careers.detail: Explain an idea to a partner and check what they actually understood.

careers.title: Observing cooperation
careers.detail: Join an ongoing task and record whether time and energy make it manageable.

careers.title: Observing checking
careers.detail: Check a small deliverable and identify conditions that affected the result.

careers.title: Trying a handover
careers.detail: Continue someone else’s work and record missing information and needed support.

careers.title: Collaboration feedback
careers.detail: Ask participants for one helpful behaviour and one that needed improvement.

careers.title: Comparing contexts
careers.detail: Compare two similar tasks and identify differences in actual conditions.

careers.title: A complete small task
careers.detail: Go from start to finish, recording what you enjoyed and found difficult.

experiment.title: Record one event before choosing a type.
experiment.body: Choose a recent small event and note its goal, limits, your first action and outcome. Find an occasion where you acted differently and compare conditions without rushing to an identity.
experiment.phrase: “Let’s see what this situation needs. I can try this small step first, then we can review the feedback together.”
experiment.review: Review: which real condition influenced your choice? Did you notice something different from your original self-image?
